This is a game about killing orcs. The concept is simple enough, but the execution is high quality. 

The game is basically a 3rd person shooter in which you have to defend a magical rift in a castle from a horde of orcs and other monsters that are trying to get through it. If too many monsters make it to the rift you lose. 

One man against a relentless horde of monsters may not seem fair, but you have a lot of advantages. In addition to your trusty crossbow, you'll have a large arsenal of spells, traps, and guardians to help out. Furthermore you earn skulls for completing levels, and you can then spend these skulls on further upgrading your arsenal.

At the start of each level you'll have time to plan and set up your defenses and get a feel for the layout of the area. You'll be told where the orcs are coming from, what route they are likely to take, how many waves there are, and even what monsters you can expect to come knocking down your door.

This is important because, despite the simple premise of "orcs must die," this is really a tactician's game. The first few levels you may be able to survive using just your crossbow, but as the difficulty level increases you will have to diversify your tactics or perish. You'll start facing more orcs, tougher monsters, monsters that come from multiple entrances, and even multiple rifts that must be defended simultaneously. 

I will give one bit of warning that is not mentioned in the game-- if you intend to play on the default (war mage) difficulty level as I did, in order to earn the maximum of 5 skulls per level you not only need to prevent any orcs from reaching the rift, you've also got to do it within the par time. Once you start the initial wave the timer starts, and it doesn't stop even during the "break" periods you sometimes get between waves.

The game is single player only. The graphics and music are adequate, but not AAA quality (this is an indie game, after all, and I don't expect AAA quality here).

There is a storyline which is short, simple, and entertaining. Borderlands fans will recognize the voice of Axton the Commando as the War Mage.

If you like third person shooters or defense-centered gameplay you'll like Orcs Must Die!

[h1] Overview [/h1]
[b]Orcs Must Die![/b] (OMD) is a single-player Tower Defense / Third Person Shooter hybrid developed by [i]Robot Entertainment[/i], and narrates of the endless battle between the Breach Guardians and endless Orc armies, the latter determined to conquer and lay waste to the kingdoms of Earth from another dimension. In this title, players will impersonate one of the silliest and apparently least capable War Mages, in a desperate attempt to repel now better-organized Orc attacks on the fortresses of the Order. 

[b]One of the main reasons OMD is an excellent title lays in the way it successfully blends the two significantly different genres of TPS and Tower Defense[/b], offering equal parts exciting action and defensive strategy as baselines of its gameplay. In each of the proposed 24 levels, [b]players will find themselves elaborating tactics based on which types of traps work best in that specific structure, considering not only layout, but also environmental hazards and static machinery[/b] already present by default. 

[b]There are many ways to effectively overcome a level, limited only by individual creativity[/b] - though some are much more efficient than others. The presence of [b]trap upgrading systems rewarding perfect completions, three different skill trees granting varied passive abilities, and a great variety of traps and weapons[/b], increase the variety and complexity of gameplay. other than that, the [b]action is great to look at, with dozens of orcs flying around and dying in the most diverse ways, while the TPS part keeps players involved[/b] and an active part in how every level plays out.

This being said, OMD has [b]some flaws as well: the most prominent lays in balancing issues, with several traps being at best situational or at worst completely useless[/b], while a select number of them are the "best" ones players will find themselves using most of the time, because they are just better in most aspects. Secondly, [b]the fact Nightmare difficulty doesn't give any strategy time to elaborate a tactic, but instead forces players into rushing[/b], throwing at them hordes the second every level begins, is a [b]really bad game design choice that has no place in the Tower Defense genre[/b], where strategy and planning always come first before action. Lastly, having a Par Time criteria for having a perfect clear on a level again is something out of place for this genre as it forces players, again, to rush and complete levels in the least time possible, else risking being out of Par.

[b]Overall, OMD is an excellent, involving, fun tower defense hybrid[/b] that nails the most important gameplay components of both genres almost flawlessly, resulting in a quality title fans of both shooters and tower defense will love. [b]Offering around 12-14 hours of content to clear everything on Normal + Nightmare, excellent quality, the current price of 10€ is absolutely a steal and I can recommend getting this game full price.[/b]

[h1] Pros & Cons [/h1]

🔵 [b] Pros [/b]
+ Perfect blend of Tower Defense and TPS, offering exciting action and tactical depth at the same time.
+ Great variety of traps, machinery, weapons and passive skills to discover, upgrade and utilize on the field.
+ Well diversified enemies, each with its own strengths and weaknesses to exploit.
+ Excellent content and quality value for the current price.
+ Fluid action with satisfying physics based gore and ragdolls, looking good for a 2011 game.

🔴 [b] Cons [/b]
- Some balance problems with traps and passives, some being too strong, while others almost useless.
- Lack of strategy time on Nightmare difficulty and Par Time to achieve a perfect clear are bad game design choices.


[h1] In-Depth Breakdown [/h1]

🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis [/b]
The gameplay of Orcs Must Die is divided into Planning, Combat and Character Management.

[b]Planning[/b] is the most important phase of any level, and consists first in selecting which traps to carry in your Spellbook and use in the level: the slots are limited, so not all traps can be deployed in a single stage, selecting the right ones for the current layout is fundamental, considering also cost, initial resources, number of enemy gates, and eventually other factors. Next up, once unlocked, players are able to select one of three passive skill-trees, each specializing in different features, such as empowering traps or instead the player itself, with powerful bonuses, altering sometimes considerably how machinery, traps and skills work. On Normal and Easy difficulties, Planning phase has unlimited time and there are several during the course of a level, to sell traps, change layouts, and fine-tuning the formation. On Nightmare instead, this part is completely removed, forcing players to deploy traps and elaborate a strategy while enemies are already coming.

[b]Combat[/b] focuses equally on player skill and trap efficiency to overcome a level, this is especially true on Nightmare difficulty: on one side, well-placed and combined traps will fend off enemies in large part, but sometimes, especially in early waves and higher difficulties, also players will have to do their part, repelling, killing or slowing enemies enough when traps simply cannot muscle all the work yet. Mechanics like headshots, elemental weaknesses and passives empowering player-exclusive skills are all in place to make your Warmage a powerhouse on the field. Your hero can die, and that comes at a penalty on Breach Health, as if several monsters broke through, so staying alive is pretty crucial: don't expect to tank whole hordes yourself unless severely buffed with passives.

[b]Character Management[/b] comes with the already mentioned passives, costing resources to purchase and unable to being refund once approved, empowering either yourself or your deployables. Other than this, at the end of each level Skulls are awarded on a scale of 1 to 5, four based on the remaining Breach Health, while one on Par Time, meaning if players cleared all waves under a certain time limit. These skulls can be used to upgrade deployables and traps, improving their functionality in different ways unique for every trap.

🔩 [b] Performance Analysis [/b]
[u]PC Specs: RTX2080Ti, Ryzen 3900X, 32GB RAM DDR4.[/u]
The game is pretty old and should run well even on today's low-end machines without issues. There are no performance, compatibility or stability issues to note.


[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]
[b]Orcs Must Die[/b] is an overall a very good Tower Defense / TPS hybrid that boasts satisfying gameplay and overall good quality content - some design choices aren't the best but considering the larger picture, it's a solid title fans of both genres will enjoy.

Definitely one of the most dynamic and fun games I've ever played

Unlike normal Tower Defense games, Orcs Must Die allows you to freely control the game flow and engage the enemy in third person. If you get this game expecting to idle all the time, this is not the game for you. Sooner or later enemies becoming increasingly difficult to hold off with your traps, so you'll have to properly aim and fire your weapon/spell and get headshots.
Although this game was made in 2011, the core gameplay has aged well and I believe newcomers will like this game.

PROS
+ Simple story line, just straight to gameplay
+ Tactical game with numerous ways to tackle hordes of enemies
+ Engaging gameplay where you have to constantly move/shoot/cast/place traps
+ Varied death animations depending on which trap was triggered

CONS
+ You don't really know what a trap can do until you actually try using it and seeing the effects for yourself
+ Trap placement is sometimes weird - cannot place a trap in certain places even when it looks like you can
+ Enemy AI is weird - sometimes even if you block off a route the enemy would just break through it, even though there's a clear alternative path it can take
+ Enemy diversity is a bit limited, such as FROST OGRE, FIRE OGRE, ARMORED OGRE

Nightmare mode is extremely punishing - the difficulty spike is insane compared to war mage. You only get 3 seconds of free time per wave with tankier and stronger enemies. I had lots of frustrations going through the levels so if that's not your cup of tea, just ignore them and play whatever you want to your hearts content!

Keep in mind this is an Indie game made in 2011. Its not a perfect game but the overall enjoyment outshadows the problems. Solid game overall.

[b]This is a long review so if you want just a brief summary of why I recommend Orcs Must Die! then skip to [u]Results[/u] and read from there.[/b]

Robot Entertainment mixes elements of different game types to conjure up a brilliant rendition of the tower defense genre. Taking action packed battles and mixing them with strategy you get a game that pushes both hack ‘n slash as well as base management. 

[b]Story:[/b]
The order has fallen, the last War Mage is dead, and protecting the realm is now left up to you his apprentice. You must fight your way through the unlimited hordes of orcs as you defend the rifts from falling into the wrong hands. As you press through your adventure you come to learn the evil forces are being led by a corrupted War Mage who plans to destroy humanity. Will you be able to save the world from falling into darkness? 

[b]Campaign:[/b]
The campaign is broken down into three acts. The first act has ten levels, the second act has 8, and the third act has 6. Despite each act having fewer levels than the last they are all about the same length as the number of waves increases throughout the campaign. Each level unlocks a new element to the game and once you’ve completed the level you gain the new item for any preceding or future level. Each time you beat a level you get a rating of one to five skulls, unlike most games these skulls actually are given to you as a currency which you can use to upgrade items. You can only get five skulls per level, meaning you cannot beat a level scoring five skulls then play it again to get another five skulls. Each level you can choose from a mastery tree that allows you to kit yourself out for that level, based on your strategies this can vary greatly throughout the campaign. You will progressively unlock more tower/item slots, which start as you only being able to equip three towers/items but later on you’ll find yourself with 10+ slots. You play the entire game in third person, and similar to other games of the genre you are able to join in the battle and help your towers out. This means you are not just sitting there waiting between waves, but rather taking an active part into the gameplay. Some levels you may find yourself not needing to join in, while others you will be right in the fray. 

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
Each level allows you to equip an inventory which allows you to choose from a combination of spells, weapons, and towers. There are two weapons (crossbow and bladestaff), four spells (flame bracers, ice amulet, lightning ring, and wind belt), two guardians (paladins and archers), and 17 towers. I found myself typically sticking to the same set throughout the entire campaign, but there are many different strategies you can go for. By placing player activated traps you can take a large part of the game, you can sit back and use guardians to do most of the work, or even mix and match. The gameplay is fast paced and really pulls you into the mix by getting you to experience new elements each level. 

[b]Artifacts of Power DLC:[/b]
Artifacts of Power is a DLC that includes new items and towers. The DLC includes two traps (Shock Zapper and Floor Scorcher) and two spells (Vampiric Gauntlets and Alchemist Satchel). I used the Floor Scorcher and Vampiric Gauntlets a few times, found the Shock Zapper completely useless (as you need a roof for it to function), and used the Alchemist Satchel to get a +50 kill streak for the achievement. All and all this DLC isn’t exactly necessary, but if you can get it on sale and included in the pack it’s worth grabbing. 

[b]Lost Adventures DLC:[/b]
Lost Adventures is a DLC that includes new level, enemies, and even a new tower. There are five new levels, which offer more skulls allowing for even more upgrades. There are two new enemies the Frost Bat, and Cyclops Mage. It also includes one new trap the mana well which allows you to refill your mana gauge. This DLC is completely worth it as it adds additional content, new enemies, towers, and refined leaderboards. If you can get this on sale or in the bundle you will not regret it. 

[b]Results:[/b]
Orcs Must Die is an epic tower defense hack ‘n slash game that keeps you pressed and wanting more. With rating systems that actually give you rewards, fun and interesting enemies, a long and arduous campaign, and an amusing little story Orcs Must Die is a Must Buy (too easy). If you are looking for something similar to Sang-Froid or Sanctum this is pretty much in that line. Once you beat Orcs Must Die you’ll feel like you need to buy the second one as it makes you just want to play more. 

Pros:
+Leaderboard system that allows you to rank yourself amongst friends.
+Level rating out of five skulls which can then be used to buy upgrades.
+Loads of spells, weapons, and towers to choose from.
+Skill trees which can be customized each level to allow you to change how you play (more player intensive, tower support, or mixture of both).
+Smooth graphics which look good and don’t push it too far.
+Funny and amusing dialogue which gives you a laugh without being offensive.
+Intense amount of action, keeps you pressed and fighting between each wave.
+Built in level traps (such as rolling locks, acid pots, lava pots, and ballista).

Cons:
-I had a few levels glitch where an enemy wouldn’t leave the spawn point and thus I couldn’t kill it requiring me to restart (this was annoying if it was at the end of the level).
-If Gnoll Hunters fall into acid pits they do not die (as I learned when I set up a level that used nearby acid pits to kill enemies). 
-One of the DLC levels (Reverse Tower) is just The Tower in Reverse. I know this is obvious from the title, but if you purchase the DLC before playing the game its disappointing to find out one of the levels is the same thing just backwards.

Orcs Must Die! is a simple game about killing orcs and killing lots of them. The game plays like a third-person shooter with tower defence mechanics that allows you to place different kinds of traps that will assist you in the killing of orcs. Whether you prefer to play more actively and shoot down as many orcs yourself, or invent trap combinations that will do most of the heavy lifting for you is up to you, and there is a good variety of weapons and traps to choose from to experiment with.

Despite being over 10 years old at this point, Orcs Must Die! holds up extremely well, visually, thanks to its cartoony aesthetic. The music, sounds and voice acting is all well done and adds greatly to the overall experience. My only complaints with this game would probably come from some missing settings I would have liked to see, such a windowed fullscreen mode and a separate audio slider for voices amongst some other things. There are also some quality of life features missing that have been implemented in the later entries, but none of these are dealbreakers in any way to me. In my opinion, the first Orcs Must Die! is a timeless classic and I'd still consider it the best game in the series, at least if you care more about the single-player experience. If you're looking to play this with a friend, this is not the game for you. Go get OMD2 or 3 instead, in that case.

Preface: Keep in mind that I am going to review this game... without the DLCs. They're not bad. It's just that I haven't bought them... yet. Even though I've had Orcs Must Die for a while.

 The story of the game is about a young-adult, sarcastic, nameless Warmage who's defending rifts in dungeons, which is gateways to the Warmages' medieval world, against waves of Orcs.
 I do not wish to spoil any quotes or scenes from the game, because that would just ruin everything.

 The gameplay is Tower-Defence... but not in a traditional way with a birds-eye-view. You play as the Warmage in 3rd person, like Gears of War(except, you can't take cover).
 You run around in the dungeon, place traps and choose which weapon and spell you are going to choose for the wave.
 At the end of each wave, you are presented with a high-score. Depending on how well you played, you will earn orc-skulls to level up your traps/magics/weapons.

Orcs Must Die! is a really fun mix of action and tower defense with a colorful, cartoony art style that still holds up pretty well. It’s simple to get into but surprisingly addictive once you start experimenting with traps. Most of the gameplay revolves around building ridiculous trap corridors and then jumping in yourself to clean up whatever enemies make it through. The game is also balanced really well for solo play, so levels feel challenging without becoming frustrating. The maps are straightforward, the pacing stays fast, and pulling off a perfect trap setup is incredibly satisfying.

That said, the game definitely shows its age in a few areas. There’s no co-op mode, there’s less content and variety compared to the sequel, and some maps can start to feel a little repetitive after a while. The humour and voice lines can also wear thin pretty quickly. Even so, it’s still a polished and addictive single-player game that’s very easy to recommend.

Story elements are fun though the connection of the levels could have used a campaign map of sorts as to why/how we move between these locations in the first place. Each level has a certain best possible path of using traps to ace it. But the good thing is that this is not mandatory and you can experiment too. Often you will find creative, or weird, uses for traps and master the levels your own way. While some levels let you build up your defences evenly others you just have to run a couple of times to know what enemies will spawn in which door. Your skill counts in not just the strategic placement of traps. But also delivering headshots is a great way to get enemies down quick, if your aim is good. Personally I love the crossbow. Mixed with the flame bracers the fighting felt really satisfying. While this worked for ME the choice is entirely yours, I believe most weapon & trap combinations can work. There are Apprentice, War Mage and Nightmare difficulties but the last one has to be unlocked. This is good because you do not get real breaks between waves in it and upgraded traps are needed. Speaking of which you can upgrade each trap using skulls you win by finishing the levels. However, the number of skulls you can get is fixed and upgrading is permanent so choose wisely based on what you like/use. The funky archer (& some trap) placement get in the way sometimes when you want to hurry but you need to keep shifting your cursor or the player to find a spot. This is annoying especially on Nightmare where you have limited time. Also the AI pathing is a bit weird but this can be both advantage and disadvantage (barricades FTW!). There's no cooperative mode though you can find that in the sequel Orcs Must Die! 2. The plus side is that you can finish this game yourself, as it was designed, while OMD!2 is more difficult to do on your own. Overall it's a good mix of tower defense and third-person action. Designed for people who like to place traps/units but don't just want to sit by and watch. Definitely worth a try.

Greetings Everyone!  So, Orcs Must Die is a bit of an oldie but I still enjoyed my time through memory lane with it.  If you didn’t know OMD is kind of a tower defense game where you play as a War Mage; someone who has access to spells, weapons and traps to defeat waves of orcs that are trying to get to your heart.  If they get to it they will damage it so it is your job to use your tools to kill them before they do.

Death to Orcs:  As the title suggests your primary goal is to kill orcs…a lot.  But you have a few interesting ways to do this.  Yes you can shoot or stab them but the primary point of the game is to use traps you set up to combo and kill them for more points.  I find this more enjoyable than even shooting them and enjoyed creating interesting combos to bounce orcs around into amusing death contraptions.

Need not Apply:  One minor gripe I have for this game is how limited it is; this is primarily fixed in the sequel (spoiler alert) but you are really only given weapons to tidy up and it is next to impossible to play as a dedicated ‘fighter’.  In addition, aside from the campaign and some DLC missions there really isn’t much to do unless you like leader boards.  The game doesn’t come with any multiplayer but I find myself not really caring all that much…the game is still very fun to play!

Look how Awesome I am:  The game has a story; albeit a small one.  One that I actually enjoyed and was amused with; of course you could argue for more but I feel the game completed exactly what it was trying to do.  Not sure how I’d improve on the raw mechanics aside from some of the issues I mentioned above.  Most of which are hindsight kind of issues; ones that I don’t think you’d think of until after the first game was finished.

After all is said and done I feel this is one of those games you just need in your library.  Sale or not I’d buy it and play around with it; even if you aren’t a tower defense player you may find something here you like.  Although, if you want to play with your friends you may just want to skip to the sequel which I feel improved on the game in every way.

Absolute banger of a game. Orcs Must Die! excels in almost every game aspect. The animations, visual style, streak, combo and headshot popups, are very satisfying to see. The soundtrack adds to the adrenaline pumping action, with lots of drums, electric guitar, harpsichord, organ, flutes, choir, etc. playing all kinds of memorable melodies. If slaughtering trillions of orcs using deadly traps, wit, and crossbow in a medieval fantasy setting had a sound, this is what it would sound like.
The game has lots of traps, but one is pretty much essential, namely the barricade, which is used to block paths and force the orcs into a choke point. Really satisfying to hoard all the orcs and slice, burn, skewer, AND launch them all at once! Different traps can be placed on the floor, wall or ceiling.
The game has almost 30 levels in total with the DLC. Lots of different layouts. with stairs, corners, pits, bridges, overpasses, and such.
As you can expect from a tower defense, it has a diverse set of enemies, that require different tactics. from small kobold runners to large ogres, flying enemies, bombers that go for the barricades.

The biggest problem in this game is its low replayability. Once you finish all levels, there's not much reason to go back, and I almost forgot to write a review as a result. Still, looking back at it, I only have fun memories. So OMD is a real no-brainer as far as game purchases are concerned. Buy it, play it, and go kill those orcs!

I realize I used the word "lots" a lot! but that word accurately encapsulates the feeling you get from this game.

Can't wait for the newest entry Orcs Must Die! Deathtrap, which will be released in January 2025.

A wonderful mix of action and setting up traps, offering enough variety even for people who aren't into Tower Defence, like me. The graphics and the story are simple but charming, the music is enthusiastic, the gameplay is amazing. The best part about the game is that even for harder levels there isn't just one optimal way to beat it, different people would have different approaches and favorite combos, unlike some Tower Defence games where with difficulty there's only one optimal solution. Here you get to have fun and feel smart doing it.

This is a really great and fun tower defense game mixed with real-time action game... once you get the hang of it. Not to imply that it isn't fun right out of the gate, but it doesn't take very long for you to sort of realize that the game wants to be played in a very particular way, and if you aren't picking up the game's hints, it can get frustrating. There are frankly a lot of things about this game that are VERY USEFUL INFORMATION that it doesn't do a particularly good job of explaining to you. Here are just a few examples of things that are confusing and will drive players to consult ye olde Google:

1. How in the hell does the skull system work...???
2. I'm kicking a** and no orcs are getting into the rift, but I keep getting low scores...???
3. I have no idea what I'm supposed to do with this steam trap...???

Here are the short versions to those answers:

1. For 5 skulls, beat the level, get lots of combos, don't lose any rift points, and beat the mysterious "target time" that you have no idea exists or what the specific target time is unless you finish the level and select "statistics" from the end-of-level options then look for the fine print.

2. Combos. It's not enough to just kill all the orcs and keep them away from the rift. You have to kill lots of orcs simultaneously, really fast, as much as possible.

3. The steam trap is a worthless piece of crap that does nothing useful (and it's not the only one). Just ignore it.

If you want to head down the path of victory instead of the path of what-the-hell-is-going-on, then here is where you should start:

1. Wind Bracers
2. Archers
3. Tar pits
4. Barricades
6. Ice amulet
7. Steel Weaver -> Death Augmenter

You'll unlock these as you progress, but those are probably the most useful traps in the game. Orcs plodding slowly through a snaking trail of tar while 15 archers fire flaming arrows at them simultaneously? While you simultaneously use the bracers to blow huge crowds of them into a lava/acid pit? Victory.

You'll pick up more tricks and variations as you go. Swinging mace trap + tar pits = virtually unstoppable. Expensive, but heavenly.

Are fliers a problem? Or maybe ogres? Or maybe hunters? ICE AMULET THOSE A-HOLES.

It's really fun once you get the feel for it and find the optimal strategies, but aspects of the game can definitely feel mysterious and frustrating at first.

This "hero" can use traps of all sorts to halt the horde's march, the only problem is that the dude is coocoo. Yup, you are the most stupid protagonist in gaming for this one... TLDR:  Enjoyable tower defense game that doesn't take itself too seriously.

When the old master war mage suffers an accidental--and embarrassing--death, it's up to his apprentice to turn back the tides and stuff the orcs back in their hole ... only, he has no idea what he's doing.

Orcs Must Die is a tower defense game like many others, of twenty-some levels split into three acts, with some amusing cinematics between them. The levels consist of barred doors with the orcs beating at the other side, and long castle corridors leading to the mysterious rifts. The player has time to lay traps, assign guardians, and so on before launching the assault--and then when the orcs come, blast them down in 3rd-person shooter-style perspective. Head shots do extra damage, as they should.

The concept is simple but the strategy can be surprisingly deep. Some of the castles have multiple approaches to multiple rifts (one wonders who designed these things) and the player may have to deal with simultaneous assaults from different angles. This is where the strategy comes in; there are various traps to inflict damage, slow the enemy, or spring-loaded panels to fling them away. The player will also earn fire, ice, and wind attacks. Some levels feature environmental aids (hot oil cauldrons, chandeliers to be dropped, spiked logs that roll down steps) that can be used one or more times. Archer or sword guardians can be summoned. After the first act, the player will be contacted by the weavers, powerful sorceresses who offer buffs--for a price, of course.

With limited coin (and time between most waves) to place traps, planning and forethought to build a cohesive defense is key. Attempt different set-ups and don't be afraid to blow a round or two to test a strategy.The player won't get the ceiling mace (swings back and forth, crushing everything underneath it) until after the halfway point, but the mace angled along the orc approach (meaning it swings parallel to the hallways, not across) with barricades to channel the orcs under it, and tar traps to slow down attackers and keep them under the mace, are incredibly effective.

Against this will come warrior orcs (bearing shields in later levels, that nullify the first hit), archer orcs, kobald runners (who don't attack but run fast for the rift) and sappers (who detonate barricades), ogres (slow but hard to put down), hobgoblin shamans (they resurrect dead enemies), and gnoll hunters (who ignore the rift but are fast, jump barricades, and track the player and guardians). Later levels introduce flying mobs, which add a new dimension of complexity to the defenses.

All of this will take practice to perfect and no one trap will account for all enemies. The ceiling mace I mentioned, for example, won't swing fast enough to catch every kobold and ogres can survive the hits and keep coming. Again, I recommend you experiment and take chances on different defenses. The nice thing is that the levels are relatively short. I think I did all of them in under 25 minutes, and they only took that long because I spent several minutes planning my defenses. It's n easy game if you just want to play for a few minutes and mow down a horde of bad guys. There are three difficulty levels: Apprentice, War Mage, and Nightmare, with scaling difficulty.

The game loads quick and I didn't encounter any glitches, save a few odd instances enemy corpses getting tossed into the environment, where they got stuck. The graphics are animated and clean, but smooth. Sound is good and provides key notices, such as if orcs break through a certain point, or faint howls when the gnoll hunters enter the map. Also, the player's war mage has some humorous lines at the start of each level. The whole thing, in fact, has a fairly tongue in cheek feel, and I enjoyed the humor.

If the game has a failing, it is that, like most tower defense games, it can get very repetitive. Also, the deeper into the campaign you go, the less margin for error there is and the harder it is to control all the lanes of attack. One viable option is to play all the way through on Apprentice, in order to get all the traps and spells available (once granted, they remain for replays of earlier maps or other difficulties).

Steam achievements are mostly doable by players of any skill and other than those directly tied to difficulty level, they can be done on the easiest settings.

All in all, Orcs Must Die is a fun time-waster, with some good humor and interesting strategic set-ups. Recommended!

[h1] Overview [/h1]
Really fun blend of tower defence and third person shooter. The game shines on the higher difficulties where you have to make the best use of different traps and abilities, though I certainly had my favourites. It does feature very quippy marvel-esque humour which was fresh for the time it came out, but may not be as enjoyable for you now. 

[h1] Steam Deck [/h1]
I played 100% on Steam Deck and had no issues. Controller isn't as precise as mouse + keyboard when it comes to shooting (headshots are really important) but I usually chose my build to focus on traps and guardians instead to mitigate that. 

[h1] Achievements [/h1]
Some will unlock just playing the game normally, but a lot require you to use specific traps in specific scenarios, or even no traps at all. Going for the achievements made me try a lot of things I may not have used otherwise, which is perfect for a game like this. 

The difficulty based achievements are in a bit of a weird balance. There are three difficulties: Apprentice, War Mage, and Nightmare, and while Nightmare is certainly the hardest, I actually had more problems in War Mage. There is an achievement that requires you to 5-star all the levels on War Mage, which requires you to never die, your core to take 0 damage, and to finish within a strict time limit. 

Nightmare, while far more difficult to complete, doesn't require you to 5-star anything, just to complete it. I completed some of the Nightmare levels very sloppily and still got past, where trying to 5-star the same level on War Mage could get sweaty. Not a complaint necessarily, and 5-starring everything on War Mage was great training for doing Nightmare in that regard, just an odd achievement difficulty balance without a similar achievement to 5-star Nightmare.
